notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Object storage service — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: S3 (Simple Storage Service)
Azure: Blob Storage
GCP: Cloud Storage (GCS)
notes.extra: All three: bucket-based, eventually-or-strongly-consistent, tiered. S3 has had strong read-after-write consistency since Dec 2020.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Managed Kubernetes — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service)
Azure: AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service)
GCP: GKE (Google Kubernetes Engine)
notes.extra: GKE is generally considered the most mature (Google originated Kubernetes). GKE Autopilot fully manages nodes.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Virtual machine / IaaS compute — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud)
Azure: Virtual Machines (VMs)
GCP: Compute Engine (GCE)

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Serverless functions (FaaS) — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: Lambda
Azure: Functions
GCP: Cloud Functions (and Cloud Run for containers)
notes.extra: FaaS = Function as a Service. GCP Cloud Run is request-driven containers, a middle ground between FaaS and full orchestration.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Managed relational database — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: RDS (Relational Database Service) + Aurora
Azure: Azure SQL Database, Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL
GCP: Cloud SQL + AlloyDB
notes.extra: Aurora and AlloyDB are cloud-native re-architectures of Postgres/MySQL with separated storage/compute.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Managed NoSQL key-value/document store — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: DynamoDB
Azure: Cosmos DB
GCP: Firestore (document) + Bigtable (wide-column)
notes.extra: Cosmos DB is multi-model with five tunable consistency levels. Bigtable is the GCP analog to DynamoDB at very high scale.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Cloud data warehouse — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: Redshift
Azure: Synapse Analytics → Microsoft Fabric (SaaS successor)
GCP: BigQuery
notes.extra: As of 2026 Fabric is the strategic successor to Synapse (which still ships as PaaS). BigQuery is the reference serverless warehouse: storage/compute fully separated.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Block storage for VMs — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: EBS (Elastic Block Store)
Azure: Managed Disks
GCP: Persistent Disk (+ Hyperdisk)

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Virtual network primitive — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) — regional
Azure: Virtual Network (VNet) — regional
GCP: VPC — global
notes.extra: Key difference: a GCP VPC spans all regions; subnets are regional. AWS/Azure networks are scoped to one region.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Container registry — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: ECR (Elastic Container Registry)
Azure: Azure Container Registry (ACR)
GCP: Artifact Registry (replaced Container Registry)

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Secrets management — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: Secrets Manager (+ Parameter Store)
Azure: Key Vault
GCP: Secret Manager
notes.extra: Key Vault also handles keys & certificates; AWS splits secrets (Secrets Manager) from KMS keys.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Message queue (point-to-point) — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: SQS (Simple Queue Service)
Azure: Service Bus
GCP: Pub/Sub (+ Cloud Tasks)

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Event/stream ingestion (high-throughput log) — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: Kinesis (Data Streams)
Azure: Event Hubs
GCP: Pub/Sub
notes.extra: Event Hubs is Kafka-protocol compatible. GCP uses Pub/Sub for both queueing and streaming.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Native infrastructure-as-code (IaC) — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: CloudFormation (+ CDK)
Azure: ARM templates → Bicep
GCP: Cloud Deployment Manager → Config Controller / Terraform
notes.extra: ARM = Azure Resource Manager. Terraform is the dominant cross-cloud tool regardless of native options.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Observability / metrics & logs — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: CloudWatch
Azure: Azure Monitor (Log Analytics + App Insights)
GCP: Cloud Operations (formerly Stackdriver)

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: CDN — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: CloudFront
Azure: Front Door / Azure CDN
GCP: Cloud CDN
notes.extra: CDN = Content Delivery Network. Azure Front Door also does global L7 load balancing + WAF.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Managed DNS — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: Route 53
Azure: Azure DNS (+ Traffic Manager for routing)
GCP: Cloud DNS
notes.extra: Route 53 uniquely combines DNS + health-checked routing policies in one service.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Identity & access management service — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: IAM (Identity and Access Management)
Azure: Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) + Azure RBAC
GCP: Cloud IAM
notes.extra: Azure splits identity (Entra ID — users/groups/apps) from authorization (RBAC role assignments on scopes).

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: How does the IAM authorization model differ across the three clouds?
notes.back:
AWS: JSON policies (allow/deny statements) attached to users, roles, or resources; explicit deny wins.
Azure: RBAC = role definition + assignment on a scope (management group / subscription / resource group / resource).
GCP: IAM bindings = role granted to a principal on a node of the resource hierarchy; policies inherit down.
notes.extra: RBAC = Role-Based Access Control. GCP and Azure inherit permissions down a hierarchy; AWS does not inherit (uses Organizations SCPs as guardrails instead).

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: What is the primary isolation / billing boundary in each cloud?
notes.back:
AWS: the Account
Azure: the Subscription
GCP: the Project
notes.extra: Best practice everywhere: many small boundaries (per-team/per-env), not one giant one. AWS Organizations / Azure Management Groups / GCP Folders group them.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Resource hierarchy — AWS / Azure / GCP top-to-bottom?
notes.back:
AWS: Organization → Organizational Unit (OU) → Account → Resource
Azure: Management Group → Subscription → Resource Group → Resource
GCP: Organization → Folder → Project → Resource
notes.extra: Azure's Resource Group is a mandatory grouping with no AWS/GCP equivalent (resources must live in exactly one). GCP folders can nest; AWS OUs can nest.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Org-wide permission guardrails — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: Service Control Policies (SCPs) on OUs/accounts
Azure: Azure Policy + RBAC deny assignments
GCP: Organization Policy constraints + IAM
notes.extra: SCPs set the *maximum* permissions; they don't grant, only bound. Azure Policy can also enforce config (e.g. 'only allowed regions').

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Workload identity without static keys — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: IAM Roles (incl. IRSA — IAM Roles for Service Accounts, on EKS)
Azure: Managed Identities / Workload Identity
GCP: Workload Identity / service accounts
notes.extra: All three let pods/VMs assume an identity via the platform rather than embedding long-lived credentials — the preferred pattern.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Stateful firewall primitive — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: Security Groups (stateful) + Network ACLs (stateless, subnet-level)
Azure: Network Security Groups (NSGs, stateful)
GCP: VPC firewall rules (stateful)
notes.extra: AWS is the odd one with a second *stateless* layer (NACLs). GCP firewall rules attach via network tags or service accounts, not per-NIC objects.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Private service connectivity (reach a service without traversing the internet) — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: PrivateLink
Azure: Private Link
GCP: Private Service Connect (PSC)
notes.extra: All expose a provider/SaaS service as a private endpoint inside your VPC/VNet.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Dedicated hybrid on-prem connectivity — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: Direct Connect
Azure: ExpressRoute
GCP: Cloud Interconnect
notes.extra: Private fiber, bypassing the public internet for bandwidth/latency/compliance.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Why is GCP's global VPC a meaningful trade-off vs AWS/Azure?
notes.back: One GCP VPC spans every region, so cross-region VMs share private routing with no peering. In AWS/Azure each VPC/VNet is regional, so multi-region designs need explicit peering / transit gateways.
notes.extra: Upside: simpler global topology in GCP. Downside: a larger single blast radius / fault & policy domain. AWS Transit Gateway and Azure Virtual WAN exist to stitch regional networks together.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: EKS vs AKS vs GKE — control-plane cost difference?
notes.back:
EKS: charges per cluster-hour for the control plane (~$0.10/hr) plus nodes.
AKS: control plane is free on the standard tier (pay only for nodes; paid 'Standard'/uptime-SLA tier optional).
GKE: per-cluster management fee (one free zonal cluster historically); Autopilot bills per pod resource request.
notes.extra: Pricing details drift — verify current rates before quoting. The structural point (EKS bills the control plane, AKS generally doesn't) is the durable exam-style fact.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: GKE Autopilot vs Standard (and the EKS/AKS equivalent)?
notes.back:
Autopilot: Google manages nodes; you only declare pods and pay per pod resource request — no node ops.
Standard: you manage the node pools.
EKS/AKS analog: managed node groups + AWS Fargate / ACI 'serverless' nodes.
notes.extra: Autopilot trades flexibility (no daemonsets-on-every-node freedom, fewer privileged options) for zero node management.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Serverless containers (no node management) — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: Fargate (with ECS or EKS)
Azure: Container Apps / ACI (Azure Container Instances)
GCP: Cloud Run
notes.extra: Cloud Run is the most polished 'request → container → scale-to-zero' experience; Fargate removes EC2 node ops under ECS/EKS.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: ARM-based compute options — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: Graviton (custom ARM)
Azure: Cobalt (custom) + Ampere Altra
GCP: Axion (custom ARM) + Tau T2A (Ampere)
notes.extra: ARM instances typically offer ~20–40% better price-performance for scale-out, compatible workloads. Graviton is the most mature.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: GCP VM live migration — what does it do that AWS/Azure typically don't?
notes.back: GCP can live-migrate a running VM to another host during host maintenance, with no reboot. AWS/Azure typically require a scheduled reboot/stop-start for some maintenance events.
notes.extra: Practical effect: fewer maintenance-driven interruptions on GCP for long-running stateful VMs.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Object storage tiers — AWS / Azure / GCP (hot → archive)?
notes.back:
AWS S3Azure BlobGCP GCS
StandardHotStandard
Standard-IA / One Zone-IACool / ColdNearline / Coldline
Glacier / Deep ArchiveArchiveArchive
notes.extra: IA = Infrequent Access. Colder tiers = cheaper storage but higher retrieval cost + latency, and minimum storage durations.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: S3 read-after-write consistency — what changed and when?
notes.back: Since December 2020, S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for all operations. Before that, new-object reads could be eventually consistent.
notes.extra: Old interview answers calling S3 'eventually consistent' are outdated. All three clouds' object stores are now strongly consistent for object reads.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: DynamoDB vs Cosmos DB — multi-region & consistency trade-off?
notes.back:
DynamoDB: single-region by default; Global Tables add active-active multi-region (last-writer-wins). Reads: eventually or strongly consistent.
Cosmos DB: turnkey global distribution with five consistency levels: Strong, Bounded Staleness, Session, Consistent Prefix, Eventual.
notes.extra: Cosmos DB's tunable consistency spectrum is its signature feature — you trade latency/availability against staleness per request.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Name Cosmos DB's five consistency levels (strongest → weakest).
notes.back:
1. Strong
2. Bounded Staleness
3. Session (default)
4. Consistent Prefix
5. Eventual
notes.extra: Maps cleanly onto the CAP/PACELC latency-vs-consistency tradeoff. Session is the practical default (read-your-own-writes per client).

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: BigQuery vs Redshift — core architectural difference?
notes.back:
BigQuery: fully serverless; storage and compute completely separated; you query without provisioning a cluster (pay per-byte-scanned or via slots).
Redshift: originally provisioned clusters (nodes you size and pay for); Redshift Serverless now also offered.
notes.extra: BigQuery is the reference 'no cluster to manage' warehouse. Azure's serverless analog is Fabric / Synapse serverless SQL pools.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Aurora vs AlloyDB — what are they?
notes.back:
Aurora (AWS): MySQL/Postgres-compatible engine re-built on a distributed, log-structured storage layer (6-way replicated across 3 AZs).
AlloyDB (GCP): Postgres-compatible with a similar disaggregated storage design + columnar acceleration for analytics.
notes.extra: Both decouple compute from a purpose-built storage tier for faster failover and read scaling vs vanilla managed Postgres (RDS / Cloud SQL).

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Serverless relational/DB scale-to-low options — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: Aurora Serverless v2 (auto-scales capacity units)
Azure: Azure SQL serverless / Cosmos DB serverless
GCP: Firestore & BigQuery are inherently serverless; Cloud SQL is not scale-to-zero

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Why is data egress the classic cloud cost trap?
notes.back: Inbound data is usually free, but outbound (egress) to the internet is billed per GB, and even cross-AZ and cross-region traffic is charged. Costs accrue invisibly in chatty/multi-region architectures.
notes.extra: Order of magnitude (varies): internet egress > cross-region > cross-AZ > same-AZ (often free). Design to keep traffic local; this also drives lock-in concerns.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Spot/interruptible compute — naming and behavior across clouds?
notes.back:
AWS: Spot Instances (reclaimed with 2-min warning)
Azure: Spot VMs (30-sec eviction notice)
GCP: Spot VMs (formerly Preemptible; Preemptible had a hard 24-h cap, Spot does not)
notes.extra: All offer steep discounts (up to ~60–90%) for interruptible capacity. Good for batch/fault-tolerant work, bad for stateful single-instance services.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Commitment-based discount models — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: Reserved Instances + Savings Plans (1- or 3-yr commit)
Azure: Reservations + Savings Plans
GCP: Committed Use Discounts (CUDs)
notes.extra: Trade upfront/term commitment for ~30–70% off on-demand. AWS Savings Plans are more flexible (commit $/hr, not a specific instance).

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: What automatic discount is unique to GCP?
notes.back: Sustained Use Discounts (SUDs): GCP automatically discounts Compute Engine VMs that run for a large fraction of the month — no commitment or action required.
notes.extra: AWS/Azure require an explicit Reserved/Savings commitment to get comparable discounts; GCP applies SUDs by default on top of (separate from) CUDs.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Define Region vs Availability Zone (AZ).
notes.back:
Region: a geographic area (e.g. eu-west-1) containing multiple isolated data-center groups.
Availability Zone (AZ): one or more discrete data centers within a region with independent power/cooling/network, low-latency linked to peer AZs.
notes.extra: Deploy across ≥2–3 AZs for HA within a region; across regions for disaster recovery / data residency. GCP calls AZs 'zones'.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Which cloud has the most 'global' (non-regional) resources, and give examples?
notes.back: GCP leans most global: the VPC is global, Cloud Load Balancing offers a single global anycast IP, Cloud Storage buckets can be multi-region. AWS/Azure keep most resources regional; AWS exposes a few global services (IAM, Route 53, CloudFront).
notes.extra: Global resources simplify multi-region but widen blast radius and complicate data-residency control.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Load balancer types — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: ALB (L7), NLB (L4), GLB/CLB
Azure: Application Gateway (L7), Azure Load Balancer (L4), Front Door (global L7)
GCP: Cloud Load Balancing (single product, global or regional, L4/L7)
notes.extra: ALB = Application LB, NLB = Network LB. GCP's global L7 LB with one anycast IP is a distinctive selling point.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Encryption at rest — what's true across all three clouds?
notes.back: All three encrypt at rest by default with platform-managed keys. You can optionally supply customer-managed keys (CMK) via the KMS: AWS KMS / Azure Key Vault / Cloud KMS.
notes.extra: Trade-off: CMK gives control/revocation/audit but adds operational burden (rotation, availability of the key = availability of the data).

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Confidential computing (encrypt data in-use) — AWS / Azure / GCP?
notes.back:
AWS: Nitro Enclaves
Azure: Confidential VMs / confidential containers
GCP: Confidential VMs (AMD SEV / Intel TDX)
notes.extra: Protects memory contents even from the hypervisor/host operator — for highly sensitive workloads (keys, regulated data).

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: State the shared responsibility model in one line.
notes.back: The cloud provider secures the infrastructure (security of the cloud); the customer secures their data, identities, configs, and workloads (security in the cloud).
notes.extra: Identical in principle across AWS/Azure/GCP. The line shifts with the service model: more provider responsibility for SaaS/serverless, more customer responsibility for IaaS.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Managed service mesh — current state across clouds (2026)?
notes.back:
AWS: App Mesh is end-of-support 2026-09-30 → use VPC Lattice or ECS Service Connect.
Azure: Open Service Mesh (OSM) retired → Istio-based add-on for AKS.
GCP: Cloud Service Mesh (managed Istio, formerly Anthos Service Mesh).
notes.extra: This area churns hard — both AWS App Mesh and Azure OSM were deprecated. Istio is the converging open standard underneath GCP's and Azure's current offerings.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: When does multi-cloud actually pay off vs cost more than it's worth?
notes.back:
Pays off: regulatory/sovereignty mandates, avoiding vendor lock-in leverage, best-of-breed services (e.g. BigQuery + AWS app), M&A reality.
Costs more: doubled ops/skills, lowest-common-denominator architecture, cross-cloud egress fees, weaker per-cloud discounts, more security surface.
notes.extra: Common pragmatic stance: pick one primary cloud; stay portable at the boundaries (containers, Terraform, open formats) rather than truly running everything everywhere.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Managed/abstracted (PaaS, serverless) vs self-run (IaaS) — the core trade-off?
notes.back:
Managed: less ops, faster delivery, built-in scaling/patching — but higher per-unit cost, less control, and tighter vendor lock-in.
Self-run: full control and portability — but you own patching, scaling, HA, and on-call.
notes.extra: The decision rarely hinges on raw compute price; it hinges on the cost of the engineering time the managed service removes.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: What primarily drives vendor lock-in on a cloud?
notes.back: Not compute (that's portable) but the differentiated managed services you build against: proprietary databases (DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, BigQuery), IAM models, eventing, and especially data gravity — egress fees make moving large datasets expensive.
notes.extra: Mitigations: open formats (Parquet/Delta), Kubernetes + containers, Terraform, abstracting provider SDKs behind interfaces. Each mitigation has its own cost.

notes.deck: Cloud: AWS / Azure / GCP Concepts & Trade-offs
notes.front: Kubernetes as a portability layer — what does it equalize, and what does it NOT?
notes.back:
Equalizes: compute scheduling, deployment model, service networking inside the cluster — workloads move across EKS/AKS/GKE fairly cleanly.
Does NOT: storage (CSI drivers differ), load balancers & ingress (cloud-specific), IAM integration, and the managed databases/queues your apps actually depend on.
notes.extra: CSI = Container Storage Interface, CNI = Container Network Interface. Portability is real at the orchestration layer but leaks at every cloud-integration boundary.
